steps.title: Understand one input row
steps.change: The row N = 1, P = 2 says node 1 has parent 2. To learn whether node 1 has children, look for its value in other rows' P column. Each output row will classify one N. Every node stays in the result. BST is the only source because each row is one node with its parent; classifying a node needs only its own N/P values and a subquery over that same node list.
steps.added_sql: SELECT N, P FROM BST ORDER BY N;
steps.sql: SELECT N, P FROM BST ORDER BY N;

steps.title: Identify the root first
steps.change: P IS NULL identifies the node with no parent. Test this first because a single-node tree also has no children and must receive the Root label.
steps.added_sql: SELECT N, P FROM BST WHERE P IS NULL;
steps.sql: SELECT N, P FROM BST WHERE P IS NULL;

steps.title: Build the known parent list
steps.change: A value used in P has at least one child. Remove NULL here so NOT IN can decide whether a node is absent from this list.
steps.added_sql: SELECT P FROM BST WHERE P IS NOT NULL ORDER BY P;
steps.sql: SELECT P FROM BST WHERE P IS NOT NULL ORDER BY P;

steps.title: Identify leaves
steps.change: Check which N values are absent from the known parent list. Those nodes have no children.

steps.title: Combine the rules
steps.change: Use CASE to check Root first, Leaf second, then return Inner for the remaining nodes. Apply ORDER BY N to produce the required ordering.
steps.added_sql:
SELECT N,
       CASE
           WHEN P IS NULL THEN 'Root'
           WHEN N NOT IN (
               SELECT P
               FROM BST
               WHERE P IS NOT NULL
           ) THEN 'Leaf'
           ELSE 'Inner'
       END AS NodeType
FROM BST
